summary: A senator whose fundraising lags puts a mortgage on his half of the family townhouse to lend his campaign money.
realLife: In December 2003 a presidential candidate planned to take a large mortgage on his half of a Boston townhouse he owned jointly with his wife and put his own money into the campaign. His campaign manager presented it as proof of his commitment. His wife's far larger wealth sat in trusts in her own name, and campaign finance law kept him from using it.
gates: The candidate owns a share of a home.
weights: Whether donors read the loan as commitment or desperation.
How far behind the campaign is.
inGame: A home and mortgage, campaign money, marriage and household money could carry it; a candidate's loan to the campaign needs a campaign loan record secured by property.

turns.what: The candidate raises enough from donors that no loan is needed.
turns.pulledBy: A surge in giving, an early win.

turns.what: The race is lost and the household carries the mortgage payments afterward.
turns.writesBack: Election loss; household debt stays; a note in the news.

turns.what: The spouse refuses to sign and the candidate lends a smaller sum from savings.
turns.pulledBy: A spouse who keeps finances apart.
turns.writesBack: Smaller loan; a quarrel on record.
